claim: Forty-nine healthy English speakers completed the experiment (17 females; 18–55 years, median: 23 years).
source: Forty-nine healthy English speakers completed this experiment (17 females; 18–55 years, median: 23 years).
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of participants, their demographics, and age range.

claim: Subjects chose a snack food item from choice sets with 9, 16, 25, or 36 items.
source: In each of 200 choice trials, subjects (N = 49) chose which snack food they would like to eat at the end of the experiment, out of a set of either 9, 16, 25, or 36 alternatives (50 trials per set size condition; see Figure 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design with specific set sizes.

claim: There were 50 trials per set size condition.
source: In each of 200 choice trials, subjects (N = 49) chose which snack food they would like to eat at the end of the experiment, out of a set of either 9, 16, 25, or 36 alternatives (50 trials per set size condition; see Figure 1 and Materials and methods).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of trials per condition.

claim: Eye movements were recorded during the choice task.
source: We recorded subjects' choices, RTs, and eye movements.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states that eye movements were recorded.

claim: Subjects rated each food on an integer scale from −3 (i.e., not at all) to 3 (i.e., very much) to indicate how much they would like to eat each item at the end of the experiment.
source: After the choice task, subjects also rated each food on an integer scale from −3 (i.e., not at all) to 3 (i.e., very much) to indicate how much they would like to eat each item at the end of the experiment (for an overview of the liking rating distributions, see Figure 1—figure supplements 1, 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the rating task and scale used.

claim: Liking ratings are used as a measure of item value.
source: We use these liking ratings as a measure of item value.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states how liking ratings are interpreted in the analysis.

claim: The probability that participants looked at an item in a choice set increased with the item's liking rating.
source: The probability that participants looked at an item in a choice set increased with the item's liking rating, while decreasing with set size (Figure 2A–D; β = 2.0%, 94% HDI = [1.6, 2.3] per rating, β = −1.4%, 94% HDI = [−1.5, –1.3] per item) (in line with recent empirical findings: Cavanagh et al., 2019; Gluth et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between looking probability and item rating.

claim: The probability that participants looked at an item decreased with set size.
source: The probability that participants looked at an item in a choice set increased with the item's liking rating, while decreasing with set size (Figure 2A–D; β = 2.0%, 94% HDI = [1.6, 2.3] per rating, β = −1.4%, 94% HDI = [−1.5, –1.3] per item) (in line with recent empirical findings: Cavanagh et al., 2019; Gluth et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between looking probability and set size.

claim: The probability that participants' gaze returned to an item increased with the item's rating.
source: Similarly, the probability that participants' gaze returned to an item increased with the item's rating while decreasing with set size (Figure 2A–D; β = 1.6%, 94% HDI = [1.4, 1.8] per rating, β = −0.65%, 94% HDI = [−0.74, –0.55] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between return gaze probability and item rating.

claim: Gaze durations increased with the item's rating.
source: Gaze durations also increased with the item's rating (Figure 2E–H; β = 11 ms, 94% HDI = [8, 13] per rating) as well as over the course of a trial (β = 0.79 ms, 94% HDI = [0.36, 1.25] per additional gaze in a trial), while decreasing with set size (β = −1.17 ms, 94% HDI = [−1.39, –0.94] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between gaze duration and item rating.

claim: Gaze durations increased over the course of a trial.
source: Gaze durations also increased with the item's rating (Figure 2E–H; β = 11 ms, 94% HDI = [8, 13] per rating) as well as over the course of a trial (β = 0.79 ms, 94% HDI = [0.36, 1.25] per additional gaze in a trial), while decreasing with set size (β = −1.17 ms, 94% HDI = [−1.39, –0.94] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between gaze duration and trial progression.

claim: Gaze durations decreased with set size.
source: Gaze durations also increased with the item's rating (Figure 2E–H; β = 11 ms, 94% HDI = [8, 13] per rating) as well as over the course of a trial (β = 0.79 ms, 94% HDI = [0.36, 1.25] per additional gaze in a trial), while decreasing with set size (β = −1.17 ms, 94% HDI = [−1.39, –0.94] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between gaze duration and set size.

claim: Initial gazes to an item were generally shorter in duration than all later gazes to the same item in the same trial.
source: Initial gazes to an item were generally shorter in duration than all later gazes to the same item in the same trial (Figure 2I–L; β = –44 ms, 94% HDI = [37, 51] difference between initial and returning gazes).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results comparing initial and returning gaze durations.

claim: Last gaze durations to the chosen item were in general longer than last gaze durations to non-chosen items.
source: Interestingly, the duration of the last gaze in a trial was dependent on whether it was to the chosen item or not (Figure 2I–L): last gaze durations to the chosen item were in general longer than last gaze durations to non-chosen items (β = 162 ms, 94% HDI = [122, 201] difference between last gazes to chosen and non-chosen items).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results comparing last gaze durations for chosen vs. non-chosen items.

claim: Subjects generally started their search in the centre of the choice screen, coinciding with the fixation cross.
source: In general, subjects began their search at the centre of the screen (Figure 3A,B; as indicated by regression coefficients close to 0 for the items' row and column positions in the beginning of a trial), coinciding with the preceding fixation cross.
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of visual search trajectories showing initial fixation patterns.

claim: Subjects typically transitioned to the top left corner after starting at the center.
source: Subjects then typically transitioned to the top left corner (Figure 3A,B; as indicated by increasingly negative regression coefficients for the items' row and column positions in the beginning of a trial) and then moved from top to bottom (Figure 3B; as indicated by the then increasingly positive regression coefficients for the items' row positions).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of visual search trajectories showing movement patterns.

claim: Over the course of the trial, subjects generally focused their search more on highly rated items.
source: Over the course of the trial, subjects generally focused their search more on highly rated (Figure 3C) and larger (Figure 3D) items, while the probability that their gaze returned to an item also steadily increased (Figure 3E; β = 9.9%, 94% HDI = [9.2, 10.7] per second, β = −0.73, 94% HDI = [−0.80, –0.66] per item), as did the durations of these returning gazes (Figure 3F; β = 14 ms, 94% HDI = [12, 17] per second, β = −2.9 ms, 94% HDI = [−3.3, –2.5] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of visual search trajectories showing attention to highly rated items over time.

claim: Over the course of the trial, subjects generally focused their search more on larger items.
source: Over the course of the trial, subjects generally focused their search more on highly rated (Figure 3C) and larger (Figure 3D) items, while the probability that their gaze returned to an item also steadily increased (Figure 3E; β = 9.9%, 94% HDI = [9.2, 10.7] per second, β = −0.73, 94% HDI = [−0.80, –0.66] per item), as did the durations of these returning gazes (Figure 3F; β = 14 ms, 94% HDI = [12, 17] per second, β = −2.9 ms, 94% HDI = [−3.3, –2.5] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports analysis of visual search trajectories showing attention to larger items over time.

claim: The probability that gaze returned to an item steadily increased over the course of the trial.
source: Over the course of the trial, subjects generally focused their search more on highly rated (Figure 3C) and larger (Figure 3D) items, while the probability that their gaze returned to an item also steadily increased (Figure 3E; β = 9.9%, 94% HDI = [9.2, 10.7] per second, β = −0.73, 94% HDI = [−0.80, –0.66] per item), as did the durations of these returning gazes (Figure 3F; β = 14 ms, 94% HDI = [12, 17] per second, β = −2.9 ms, 94% HDI = [−3.3, –2.5] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing return gaze probability over time.

claim: The durations of returning gazes increased over the course of the trial.
source: Over the course of the trial, subjects generally focused their search more on highly rated (Figure 3C) and larger (Figure 3D) items, while the probability that their gaze returned to an item also steadily increased (Figure 3E; β = 9.9%, 94% HDI = [9.2, 10.7] per second, β = −0.73, 94% HDI = [−0.80, –0.66] per item), as did the durations of these returning gazes (Figure 3F; β = 14 ms, 94% HDI = [12, 17] per second, β = −2.9 ms, 94% HDI = [−3.3, –2.5] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing return gaze duration over time.

claim: The fraction of total trial time that subjects looked at an item was dependent on the liking rating of the item.
source: Overall, the fraction of total trial time that subjects looked at an item was dependent on the liking rating, size, and position of the item, as well as the number of items contained in the choice set (β = 0.5%, 94% HDI = [0.4, 0.6] per liking rating, β = 0.02%, 94% HDI = [0.008, 0.03] per percentage increase in size, β = −0.20%, 94% HDI = [−0.24, –0.15] per row position, β = −0.044, 94% HDI = [−0.075, –0.007] per column position, β = −0.177, 94% HDI = [−0.18, –0.174] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between cumulative gaze and item attributes.

claim: The probability of choosing an item did not depend on the size or position of the item.
source: We also tested whether these item attributes influenced subjects' choice behaviour. However, the probability of choosing an item did not depend on the size or position of the item, but was solely dependent on the item's liking rating and the set size (β = 3.9, 94% HDI = [3.5, 4.3] per liking rating, β = 0.02, 94% HDI = [−0.015, 0.06] per percentage increase in item size, β = −0.06, 94% HDI = [−0.12, 0.01] per row, β = −0.03, 94% HDI = [−0.1, 0.03] per column, β = −0.24, 94% HDI = [−0.25, –0.23] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing that item size and position do not predict choice.

claim: The probability of choosing an item was dependent on the item's liking rating and the set size.
source: We also tested whether these item attributes influenced subjects' choice behaviour. However, the probability of choosing an item did not depend on the size or position of the item, but was solely dependent on the item's liking rating and the set size (β = 3.9, 94% HDI = [3.5, 4.3] per liking rating, β = 0.02, 94% HDI = [−0.015, 0.06] per percentage increase in item size, β = −0.06, 94% HDI = [−0.12, 0.01] per row, β = −0.03, 94% HDI = [−0.1, 0.03] per column, β = −0.24, 94% HDI = [−0.25, –0.23] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing that item rating and set size predict choice.

claim: Subjects chose the highest-rated item that they looked at in all set sizes at a very consistent rate across set sizes.
source: Conditional on the set of looked-at items, subjects chose the highest-rated item at a very consistent rate across set sizes (Figure 4A; β = 0.05%, 94% HDI = [−0.04, 0.14] per item), with an overall average of 84%.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing choice accuracy across set sizes.

claim: Subjects did not look at all food items in a given trial.
source: However, subjects did not look at all food items in a given trial (Figure 4B), while the fraction of items in a choice set that subjects looked at decreased across set sizes (Figure 4B; β = −1.52%, 94% HDI = [−1.60, –1.45] per item) and their mean RTs increased (Figure 4C; β = 85 ms, 94% HDI = [67, 102] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports observational data showing incomplete search behavior.

claim: The fraction of items in a choice set that subjects looked at decreased across set sizes.
source: However, subjects did not look at all food items in a given trial (Figure 4B), while the fraction of items in a choice set that subjects looked at decreased across set sizes (Figure 4B; β = −1.52%, 94% HDI = [−1.60, –1.45] per item) and their mean RTs increased (Figure 4C; β = 85 ms, 94% HDI = [67, 102] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between fraction of items looked at and set size.

claim: Mean response times increased with set size.
source: However, subjects did not look at all food items in a given trial (Figure 4B), while the fraction of items in a choice set that subjects looked at decreased across set sizes (Figure 4B; β = −1.52%, 94% HDI = [−1.60, –1.45] per item) and their mean RTs increased (Figure 4C; β = 85 ms, 94% HDI = [67, 102] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between response time and set size.

claim: Subjects did not look at all items before making a choice, which ruled out a strict interpretation of the optimal choice model.
source: This immediately ruled out a strict interpretation of the optimal choice model, as subjects did not look at all items before making a choice.
evidence: The manuscript draws an inference from the observation that subjects did not look at all items.

claim: Subjects chose the item that they looked at last in a trial about half the time.
source: However, across set sizes, subjects only chose the last item that they looked at in 44.6% of the trials (Figure 4D; β = 0.14%, 94% HDI = [−0.001, 0.26] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the probability of choosing the last-seen item.

claim: Within the trials where subjects did not look at every item, the probability that they chose the last-seen item was on average only 44.1%.
source: Even within the trials where subjects did not look at every item, the probability that they chose the last-seen item was on average only 44.1%.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results for a subset of trials.

claim: Both cached value and elapsed time had positive effects on subjects' stopping probability.
source: We found that both had positive effects on subjects' stopping probability, in addition to a negative effect of set size (β = 2.7%, 94% HDI = [2.0, 3.3] per cached value, β = 2.26%, 94% HDI = [1.69, 2.80] per second, β = −0.22%, 94% HDI = [−0.24, –0.20] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing factors affecting stopping probability.

claim: Set size had a negative effect on subjects' stopping probability.
source: We found that both had positive effects on subjects' stopping probability, in addition to a negative effect of set size (β = 2.7%, 94% HDI = [2.0, 3.3] per cached value, β = 2.26%, 94% HDI = [1.69, 2.80] per second, β = −0.22%, 94% HDI = [−0.24, –0.20] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the effect of set size on stopping probability.

claim: All subjects exhibited positive values on the gaze influence measure in all set sizes.
source: We found that all subjects exhibited positive values on this measure in all set sizes (Figure 4E; with values ranging from 1.7% to 75%) and that it increased with set size (Figure 4E; β = 0.26%, 94% HDI = [0.15, 0.39] per item), indicating an overall positive association between gaze allocation and choice.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing positive gaze influence across all subjects and conditions.

claim: The gaze influence measure increased with set size.
source: We found that all subjects exhibited positive values on this measure in all set sizes (Figure 4E; with values ranging from 1.7% to 75%) and that it increased with set size (Figure 4E; β = 0.26%, 94% HDI = [0.15, 0.39] per item), indicating an overall positive association between gaze allocation and choice.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between gaze influence and set size.

claim: A subject's probability of choosing an item increased with the item's cumulative gaze advantage.
source: In general, a subject's probability of choosing an item increased with the item's cumulative gaze advantage and the item's relative rating, while it decreased with the range of the ratings of the other items in a choice set and set size (β = 0.46%, 94% HDI = [0.4, 0.5] per percentage increase in cumulative gaze advantage, β = 3.6%, 94% HDI = [3.2, 4.0] per unit increase in relative rating, β = −2.8%, 94% HDI = [−3.1, –2.4] per unit increase in the range of ratings of the other items, β = −0.16, 94% HDI = [−0.18, –0.14] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between choice probability and cumulative gaze advantage.

claim: The probability of choosing the highest-rated seen item was negatively correlated with the gaze influence measure.
source: In line with this prediction, we found that probability of choosing the highest-rated seen item was negatively correlated with the gaze influence measure (β = −0.22%, 94% HDI = [−0.36, –0.08] per percentage increase in gaze influence; the mixed-effects regression included a random slope and intercept for each set size).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing a negative correlation between choice accuracy and gaze influence.

claim: Subjects with higher values on the gaze influence measure were more likely to choose the item that they looked at last in a trial.
source: In line with this prediction, subjects with higher values on the gaze influence measure (indicating stronger gaze bias) were also more likely to choose the item that they looked at last in a trial (β = 1.1%, 94% HDI = [0.9, 1.3] per percentage increase in gaze influence; the mixed-effects regression included a random slope and intercept for each set size).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between gaze influence and last-item choice.

claim: The probability of choosing the first-seen item in a trial increased with the duration of the first gaze.
source: Overall, this relationship was positive (as was the influence of the item's rating on choice probability), while the item's choice probability decreased with set size (β = 18%, 94% HDI = [14, 22] per second, β = 6.0%, 94% HDI = [5.5, 6.6] per rating, β = −0.27%, 94% HDI = [−0.32, –0.22] per item).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between first gaze duration and choice probability.

claim: Subjects with a stronger influence of rating on gaze allocation generally looked at fewer items.
source: Subjects with a stronger influence of rating on gaze allocation generally looked at fewer items (β = −17%, 94% HPI = [−30, –5] per unit increase in βgaze(rating); Figure 4—figure supplement 1H), were more likely to choose the highest-rated seen item (β = 14%, 94% HDI = [5, 23] per unit increase in βgaze(rating); Figure 4—figure supplement 1P), and were more likely to choose the last-seen item (β = 40%, 94% HDI = [19, 61] per unit increase in βgaze(rating); Figure 4—figure supplement 1T).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between rating influence on gaze and number of items looked at.

claim: The choices and RTs of the vast majority of subjects were best captured by the model variants with an active account of gaze.
source: According to the WAIC, the choices and RTs of the vast majority of subjects were best captured by the model variants with an active account of gaze (82% [40/49], 94% [46/49], 90% [44/49], and 86% [42/49] for 9, 16, 25, and 36 items respectively; Figure 5A–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports model comparison results using WAIC.

claim: The PSM+ won the plurality of individual WAIC comparisons in each set size.
source: Specifically, the PSM+ won the plurality of individual WAIC comparisons in each set size (39% [19/49], 65% [32/49], 47% [23/49], and 51% [25/49] in the sets with 9, 16, 25, and 36 items, respectively), while the plurality of the remaining WAIC comparisons was won by the GLAM+ for 9 and 16 items (29% [14/49] and 16% [8/49] subjects, respectively) and by the IAM+ for 25 and 36 items (22% [11/49] and 24% [12/49] subjects, respectively).
evidence: The manuscript reports model comparison results showing which model won most often.

claim: The WAIC distributions of the PSM+ and GLAM+ were not meaningfully different from one another in any set size.
source: This analysis revealed that the WAIC distributions of the PSM+ and GLAM+ were not meaningfully different from one another in any set size (U = 1287, p = 0.54; U = 1444, p=0.08; U = 1460, p = 0.07; U = 1469, p = 0.06 for 9, 16, 25, and 36 items), while the PSM+ was meaningfully better than the IAM+ for 16 items (U = 1705, p = 0.0003), but not for 9 (U = 1592, p = 0.005), 25 (U = 1573, p = 0.008), or 36 (U = 1508, p = 0.029) items.
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical test results comparing WAIC distributions between models.

claim: The PSM+ and GLAM+ both accurately recovered mean RT.
source: The PSM+ and GLAM+ both accurately recovered mean RT (Figure 6A,C; intercept = −138 ms, 94% HDI = [−414, 119], β = 1.01 ms, 94% HDI = [0.95, 1.05] per ms increase in observed RT for the PSM+; intercept = −51 ms, 94% HDI = [−327, 207], β = 0.97 ms, 94% HDI = [0.91, 1.06] per ms increase in observed RT for the GLAM+), while the IAM+ underestimated short and overestimated long mean RTs (Figure 6B; intercept = −1185 ms, 94% HDI = [−2293, –61], β = 1.29 ms, 94% HDI = [1.19, 1.39] per ms increase in observed RT).
evidence: The manuscript reports model validation results comparing predicted and observed RTs.

claim: The IAM+ underestimated short and overestimated long mean RTs.
source: The PSM+ and GLAM+ both accurately recovered mean RT (Figure 6A,C; intercept = −138 ms, 94% HDI = [−414, 119], β = 1.01 ms, 94% HDI = [0.95, 1.05] per ms increase in observed RT for the PSM+; intercept = −51 ms, 94% HDI = [−327, 207], β = 0.97 ms, 94% HDI = [0.91, 1.06] per ms increase in observed RT for the GLAM+), while the IAM+ underestimated short and overestimated long mean RTs (Figure 6B; intercept = −1185 ms, 94% HDI = [−2293, –61], β = 1.29 ms, 94% HDI = [1.19, 1.39] per ms increase in observed RT).
evidence: The manuscript reports model validation results showing systematic bias in IAM+ RT predictions.

claim: All three models generally underestimated high probabilities of choosing the highest-rated item from a choice set.
source: All three models generally underestimated high probabilities of choosing the highest-rated item from a choice set (Figure 6D–F), while the PSM+ provided the overall most accurate account of this metric (Figure 6D; intercept = −1.90%, 94% HDI = [−7.64, 3.19], β = 0.85%, 94% HDI = [0.79, 0.91] per percentage increase in observed probability of choosing the highest-rated item), followed by the GLAM+ (Figure 6E; intercept = 11.66%, 94% HDI = [5.27, 17.41], β = 0.71%, 94% HDI = [0.64, 0.78] per percentage increase in observed probability of choosing the highest-rated item), and IAM+ (Figure 6F; intercept = 10.48%, 94% HDI = [0.15, 28.20], β = 0.33%, 94% HDI = [0.15, 0.49] per percentage increase in observed probability of choosing the highest-rated item).
evidence: The manuscript reports model validation results comparing predicted and observed choice accuracy.

claim: The PSM+ and IAM+ both slightly overestimated weak associations between gaze and choice while clearly underestimating stronger associations between them.
source: Turning to the gaze data, the PSM+ and IAM+ both slightly overestimated weak associations between gaze and choice while clearly underestimating stronger associations between them (Figure 6G–H; intercept = 7.03%, 94% HDI = [4.95, 10.23], β = 0.48%, 94% HDI = [0.38, 0.56] per percentage increase in observed gaze influence for the PSM+; intercept = 6.58%, 94% HDI = [4.28, 10.30], β = 0.38%, 94% HDI = [0.15, 0.49] per percentage increase in observed gaze influence for the IAM+).
evidence: The manuscript reports model validation results comparing predicted and observed gaze-choice associations.

claim: The GLAM+ only slightly underestimated strong associations of gaze and choice.
source: The GLAM+, in contrast, only slightly underestimated strong associations of gaze and choice (Figure 6I; intercept = −0.61%, 94% HDI = [−2.84, 1.64], β = 0.85%, 94% HDI = [0.77, 0.93] per percentage increase in observed gaze influence).
evidence: The manuscript reports model validation results showing GLAM+ accurately captures gaze-choice associations.

claim: Evidence was found for both multiplicative and additive gaze biases in the PSM+ and GLAM+ across all set sizes.
source: We found evidence for both of these gaze biases in the PSM+ and GLAM+ across all set sizes, with mean (s.d.) γ estimates (per set size) of 9: 0.63 (0.29), 16: 0.53 (0.27), 25: 0.57 (0.27), and 36: 0.59 (0.29) for the PSM+ (Supplementary file 1) and 9: 0.72 (0.28), 16: 0.64 (0.27), 25: 0.68 (0.27), and 36: 0.71 (0.27) for the GLAM+ (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: The manuscript reports parameter estimates from model fitting showing evidence for both types of gaze bias.

claim: No evidence was found for additive gaze biases in the IAM+.
source: Interestingly, we did not find any evidence for additive gaze biases in the IAM+ (with mean [s.d.] ζ estimates of 9: 0.23 [0.69], 16: 0.20 [0.73], 25: 0.32 [0.98], and 36: 0.31 [0.72]; Supplementary file 2), while multiplicative gaze biases were more pronounced (as indicated by mean [s.d.] γ estimates of 9: 0.01 [0.05], 16: 0.005 [0.008], 25: 0.02 [0.05], and 36: 0.02 [0.09]; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports parameter estimates from model fitting showing no evidence for additive gaze bias in IAM+.

claim: In the PSM+ and GLAM+, γ estimates generally decreased with increasing ζ estimates.
source: In the PSM+ and GLAM+, γ estimates generally decreased with increasing ζ estimates (β = −0.06, 94% HDI = [−0.09, –0.03] per unit increase in ζ for the PSM+ (Figure 7A); β = −0.08, 94% HDI = [−0.10, –0.05] per unit increase in ζ for the GLAM+ (Figure 7C); the mixed-effects regressions included a random slope and intercept for each set size), such that subjects with a stronger additive gaze bias (as indicated by larger ζ estimates) generally also exhibited stronger multiplicative gaze biases (as indicated by smaller γ estimates).
evidence: The manuscript reports statistical analysis results showing the relationship between multiplicative and additive gaze bias parameters.

claim: Subjects' behaviour qualitatively could not be explained by optimal choice or standard instantiations of satisficing.
source: We found that subjects' behaviour qualitatively could not be explained by optimal choice or standard instantiations of satisficing.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from qualitative model comparisons.

claim: After incorporating active effects of gaze into a probabilistic version of satisficing, it explained the data well, slightly outperforming the evidence accumulation models in fitting choice and RT data.
source: After incorporating active effects of gaze into a probabilistic version of satisficing, it explained the data well, slightly outperforming the evidence accumulation models in fitting choice and RT data.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from quantitative model comparisons.

claim: The relative accumulation model with active gaze influences provided by far the best fit to the observed association between gaze allocation and choice behaviour.
source: Yet, the relative accumulation model with active gaze influences provided by far the best fit to the observed association between gaze allocation and choice behaviour, which was not explicitly accounted for in the likelihood-based model comparison, thus demonstrating that gaze-driven relative evidence accumulation provides the most comprehensive account of behaviour in MAFC.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from model validation analyses.

claim: Models with active gaze consistently outperform their passive-gaze counterparts in terms of overall goodness-of-fit.
source: In terms of overall goodness-of-fit, we find that the models with active gaze consistently outperform their passive-gaze counterparts.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from model comparison analyses.

claim: Gaze does more than bring an alternative into the consideration set, it actively increases the subjective value of the attended alternative relative to the others.
source: That is, gaze does more than bring an alternative into the consideration set, it actively increases the subjective value of the attended alternative relative to the others.
evidence: The manuscript interprets the finding that active gaze models outperform passive gaze models.

claim: The probabilistic satisficing model (PSM) performs slightly better than the other models at capturing individuals' choices and RTs.
source: The probabilistic satisficing model (PSM) performs slightly better than the other models at capturing individuals' choices and RTs, while the relative accumulator model provides the best overall account of the data after considering the observed positive relation between gaze allocation and choice.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from model comparison and validation analyses.

claim: The relative accumulator model provides the best overall account of the data when also considering the empirical relation between gaze allocation and choice.
source: The probabilistic satisficing model (PSM) performs slightly better than the other models at capturing individuals' choices and RTs, while the relative accumulator model provides the best overall account of the data after considering the observed positive relation between gaze allocation and choice.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings from model comparison and validation analyses.

claim: Simple value-based choices are made through a process of gaze-driven evidence accumulation and comparison, as captured by the attentional drift diffusion model and the gaze-weighted linear accumulator model.
source: Prior work on 2AFC has indicated that simple value-based choices are made through a process of gaze-driven evidence accumulation and comparison, as captured by the attentional drift diffusion model (Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Smith and Krajbich, 2019) and the gaze-weighted linear accumulator model (GLAM; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on binary choice mechanisms.

claim: Longer gaze towards one alternative should generally increase the probability that it is chosen.
source: One result of this process is that longer gaze towards one alternative should generally increase the probability that it is chosen, in line with recent empirical findings (Amasino et al., 2019; Armel et al., 2008; Cavanagh et al., 2014; Fisher, 2017; Folke et al., 2017; Gluth et al., 2018; Gluth et al., 2020; Konovalov and Krajbich, 2016; Pärnamets et al., 2015; Shimojo et al., 2003; Stewart et al., 2016; Vaidya and Fellows, 2015).
evidence: The manuscript describes a prediction from gaze-driven evidence accumulation models and cites supporting empirical findings.

claim: It is still unknown whether the gaze-driven evidence accumulation framework can account for choices from truly large choice sets.
source: While this framework can in theory be extended to MAFC (Gluth et al., 2020; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Thomas et al., 2019; Towal et al., 2013), it is still unknown whether it can account for choices from truly large choice sets.
evidence: The manuscript identifies a gap in the literature regarding the applicability of existing models to large choice sets.

claim: Past research in MAFC suggests that people may resort to a 'satisficing' strategy.
source: In contrast, past research in MAFC suggests that people may resort to a 'satisficing' strategy. Here, the idea is that people set a minimum threshold on what they are willing to accept and search through the alternatives until they find one that is above that threshold (McCall, 1970; Simon, 1955; Simon, 1956; Simon, 1957; Simon, 1959; Schwartz et al., 2002; Stüttgen et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on satisficing in many-alternative choice.

claim: Satisficing has been observed in a variety of choice scenarios, including tasks with a large number of alternatives.
source: Satisficing has been observed in a variety of choice scenarios, including tasks with a large number of alternatives (Caplin et al., 2011; Stüttgen et al., 2012), patients with damage to the prefrontal cortex (Fellows, 2006), inferential decisions (Gigerenzer and Goldstein, 1996), survey questions (Krosnick, 1991), risky financial decisions (Fellner et al., 2009), and with increasing task complexity (Payne, 1976).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing satisficing across different contexts.

claim: The best model for MAFC under strict time limits is a probabilistic version of satisficing in which the time point when individuals stop their search and make a choice follows a probabilistic function of elapsed time and cached item value.
source: Past work has also investigated MAFC under strict time limits (Reutskaja et al., 2011). There, the authors find that the best model is a probabilistic version of satisficing in which the time point when individuals stop their search and make a choice follows a probabilistic function of elapsed time and cached (i.e., highest-seen) item value (Chow and Robbins, 1961; Rapoport and Tversky, 1966; Robbins et al., 1971; Simon, 1955; Simon, 1959).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work on probabilistic satisficing models.

claim: Individuals look back and forth between alternatives as if comparing them.
source: There is some empirical evidence that points towards a gaze-driven evidence accumulation and comparison process for MAFC. For instance, individuals look back and forth between alternatives as if comparing them (Russo and Rosen, 1975).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing comparison behavior in MAFC.

claim: Frequently looking at an item dramatically increases the probability of choosing that item.
source: Also, frequently looking at an item dramatically increases the probability of choosing that item (Chandon et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing the relationship between gaze frequency and choice.

claim: Individuals use a gaze-dependent evidence accumulation process when making choices from sets of up to eight alternatives.
source: Empirical evidence has further indicated that individuals use a gaze-dependent evidence accumulation process when making choices from sets of up to eight alternatives (Ashby et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites prior work showing gaze-dependent evidence accumulation in moderate-sized choice sets.

claim: In the binary choice setting, the probability that an item was looked at did not increase with the item's rating, in contrast to the multi-alternative choice setting.
source: In contrast to the binary choice setting (Krajbich et al., 2010), we found that the probability that an item was looked at, as well as the duration of a gaze to this item, increased with the item's rating, and that this trend also increased over the course of a trial (Figures 2 and 3).
evidence: The manuscript contrasts findings from the current study with prior work on binary choice, implying a difference in gaze patterns.

claim: When deciding between two alternatives, attending to either alternative is equally useful in reaching the correct decision.
source: In a sense, the contrast between binary and multi-alternative choice is not surprising. When deciding between two alternatives, you are merely trying to compare one to the other. In that case, attending to either alternative is equally useful in reaching the correct decision.
evidence: The manuscript provides a theoretical explanation for differences between binary and multi-alternative choice.

claim: With many choice alternatives, it is in your best interest to quickly identify the best alternatives in the choice set and exclude all other alternatives from further consideration.
source: However, with many choice alternatives, it is in your best interest to quickly identify the best alternatives in the choice set and exclude all other alternatives from further consideration (e.g., Hauser and Wernerfelt, 1990; Payne, 1976; Reutskaja et al., 2011; Roberts and Lattin, 1991).
evidence: The manuscript provides a theoretical explanation for search behavior in many-alternative choice and cites supporting work.

claim: Subjects' choices are more driven by their gaze in the later stages of the decision, when they focus more on the highly rated items in the choice set, than in the earlier stages of the search.
source: Given this search and decision process, we might expect that subjects' choices are more driven by their gaze in the later stages of the decision, when they focus more on the highly rated items in the choice set, than in the earlier stages of the search, when gaze is driven by the items' positions and sizes. Indeed, we found that only the items' ratings predicted choice behaviour, not their positions or sizes.
evidence: The manuscript infers a temporal pattern in the gaze-choice relationship based on the finding that only ratings predict choice.

claim: If the experiment had included aversive snack foods, or the framing of the decision problem had been reversed, gaze would be expected to have the opposite effect.
source: As our experiment included only appetitive snack foods, both of these types of gaze biases have similar effects on the decision process, by increasing the subjective value of the currently looked-at alternative relative to the others. If, however, our experiment had included aversive snack foods, or the framing of the decision problem had been reversed (Sepulveda et al., 2020), we would have expected gaze to have the opposite effect.
evidence: The manuscript speculates about how gaze effects might differ under different experimental conditions.

claim: Subjects do not look at every item in many-alternative forced choice.
source: Overall, our findings firmly reject a model of complete search and maximization in MAFC (Caplin et al., 2011; Pieters and Warlop, 1999; Reutskaja et al., 2011; Simon, 1959; Stüttgen et al., 2012): Subjects do not look at every item, and they do not always choose the best item they have seen.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings that reject complete search models.

claim: Subjects do not always choose the best item they have seen in many-alternative forced choice.
source: Overall, our findings firmly reject a model of complete search and maximization in MAFC (Caplin et al., 2011; Pieters and Warlop, 1999; Reutskaja et al., 2011; Simon, 1959; Stüttgen et al., 2012): Subjects do not look at every item, and they do not always choose the best item they have seen.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings that reject maximization models.

claim: Subjects choose the last item they look at only half of the time, which clearly rejects the hard satisficing model.
source: Our data also clearly reject the hard satisficing model: Subjects choose the last item they look at only half of the time.

claim: Subjects' choices are strongly dependent on the actual time that they spend looking at each alternative.
source: Additionally, we find that subjects' choices are strongly dependent on the actual time that they spend looking at each alternative and can therefore not be fully explained by simply accounting for the set of examined items.
evidence: The manuscript summarizes findings showing the importance of gaze duration.

claim: Many models of consumer search and rational inattention ascribe a more passive role to visual attention, by viewing it as a filter that creates consideration sets.
source: This stands in stark contrast to many models of consumer search and rational inattention (e.g., Caplin et al., 2019; Masatlioglu et al., 2012; Matějka and McKay, 2015; Sims, 2003), which ascribe a more passive role to visual attention, by viewing it as a filter that creates consideration sets (by attending only to a subset of the available alternatives) from which the decision maker then chooses.
evidence: The manuscript contrasts findings with existing theoretical frameworks in economics.

claim: Attention takes a much more active role in MAFC by guiding preference formation within the consideration set.
source: Our findings indicate that attention takes a much more active role in MAFC by guiding preference formation within the consideration set, as has been observed with smaller choice sets (e.g., Armel et al., 2008; Gluth et al., 2020; Krajbich et al., 2010; Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Smith and Krajbich, 2019; Thomas et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript summarizes the main finding about the active role of attention and cites supporting work.

source: In conclusion, we find that models of gaze-weighted subjective value account for relations between eye-tracking data and choice that other passive-attention models of MAFC cannot.
